sub_agendas_items.title: Auditor’s Report – Election compliance audit of the campaign finances of Candidate Shawn Menard, Ward 17 Capital, from the 2022 Municipal Elections

motions.motion_text:
Report Recommendation(s)
That, pursuant to Subsection 88.33(17) of theMunicipal Elections Act, 1996, the Election Compliance Audit Committee consider the Auditor’s report and decide whether to commence a legal proceeding against Candidate Shawn Menard.

BE IT RESOLVED THAT the Committee issues the following decision and reasons:
Upon receiving report ACS2025-OCC-GEN-0010 titled “Auditor’s Report – Election compliance audit of the campaign finances of Candidate Shawn Menard, Ward 17 Capital, from the 2022 Municipal Elections” [the “Report”] and upon hearing the representations and/or reading the written submissions and documents submitted by the Auditor, the Candidate, and the Applicant’s representative, this Committee hereby decides not to commence legal proceedings against CandidateShawn Menardfor apparent contravention(s) of the election campaign finance provisions under theMunicipal Elections Act, 1996[“MEA”].
Discussion
Auditor’s Report
The Committee considered the Auditor’s Report, which concluded as follows:
With respect to the apparent violation, the Report stated that the amount recorded in the financial statement for the election campaign signs reused from the previous municipal election was inaccurate. Specifically, the Auditor found Mr. Menard understated the sign expenses by $310.98.
The Report also noted that, in his Form 4 financial statement, Mr. Menard estimated the cost of sign material used in the previous election to be $100. The Auditor considered this estimate reasonable based on its own research showing the subject materials would have cost $98.12 if procured based on prices listed by a “reputable hardware supplier”.
The Auditor noted that the apparent violation it identified does not place the Candidate above the MEA’s spending limit.
Applicant’s submissions
The Committee considered the written and oral submissions of the applicant, Edward Phillips, by his representative, Mr. John Pappas.
In summary, Mr. Pappas argued that Mr. Menard, with his prior experience from multiple elections, failed to accurately report the replacement value of reused campaign materials—specifically large election signs—in his Form 4 Financial Statement. This caused him to understate both campaign expenses and in-kind contributions, which contravened the MEA. This breach, Mr. Pappas contended, was no mere clerical oversight but a fundamental “threat” to the MEA's core objectives of transparency, accountability, and fairness. He also submitted that even “clerical errors” may give rise to a decision to refer a matter to prosecution under the MEA. For this proposition, he relied in part on a previous composition of this Committee’s decisions in matters involving Laura Dudas and Mark Taylor. He also referenced the Committee’s previous decision regarding Horizon Ottawa.
The Applicant’s submissions also criticized the Auditor for not consulting him despite his ability to provide purportedly relevant evidence.
Mr. Pappas cited the MEA’s policy goals and referenced case law, such asFrench v. Township of Springwater, 2018 ONSC 94, which described the Committee's role as a gatekeeper assessing public interest.
On thede minimisdoctrine, Mr. Pappas drew fromJackson v. Vaughan (City)(2009), 59 M.P.L.R. (4th) 55, arguing that even small dollar amounts may be a relevant consideration for the Committee’s role at this juncture.
Mr. Pappas also stated that this Committee has made decisions to commence legal proceedings in the past. For example, on March 10, 2020, the Committee voted to initiate proceedings against Laura Dudas after an external audit identified areas of non-compliance in her election finances, including the improper reporting of reused campaign materials from a prior election. Similarly, on December 14, 2015, the Committee decided to commence legal proceedings against Mark Taylor for a clerical error in his 2014 election financial statement related to inaccurately reporting a carried-over campaign deficit. In its decision, the Committee noted that errors, regardless of intent or scale, should not be overlooked.
In oral submissions, Mr. Pappas encouraged the Committee to consider the issue from the perspective of the prosecutor, noting that the one act (or omission) at issue in this case gives rise to several discrete violations of the MEA.
Mr. Menard’s submission
Mr. Menard indicated that he respected the Auditor’s findings and noted that they are consistent with what he previously stated to the Committee.
He stated that the audit was time intensive. He complied in producing all receipts, and records of expenses and contributions in his possession related to his campaign. He likewise noted that this matter has received extensive media coverage, both mainstream and on social media.
Mr. Menard submitted that in the appeal from the Committee’s previous decision at the application stage of this Matter, Regional Senior Justice MacLeod observed that small irregularities may be indicative of bigger ones that may only come to light after a compliance audit. This was one of the bases for allowing Mr. Philips’s appeal and directing this Committee to order a compliance audit. However, now that the audit has been completed, no further apparent violations were found.
He summed up his submission in stating that, in the circumstances, the public interest would not be best served by referring this matter to prosecution.
Committee’s Findings
The Committee agrees with the Auditor’s statement that there is an apparent violation of subsection 88.19(3) of the MEA. The Auditor’s Report stated that the amount recorded in the financial statement for the previous election campaign signs was inaccurate and is an apparent non-compliance of subsection 88.19(3) of the MEA. The Committee sees no reason to doubt the correctness of the Auditor’s conclusion on this point.
The Committee likewise agrees with the Auditor that, accounting for the understatement relating to signs, Mr. Menard remains within the spending limit per the MEA. The Committee also notes that Mr. Menard did not exceed the maximum contributions allowed from a candidate or his or her spouse. This is even when one accounts for the understatement of the sign values giving rise to the apparent violation at issue.
Concerning the submissions by Mr. Pappas, the Committee finds that all candidates are subject to the same regulatory requirements under the MEA and should be subject to the same level of scrutiny and accountability, regardless of whether they are first time or seasoned candidates. To the extent the Applicant’s submissions suggest Mr. Menard, as a repeat candidate should be held to a different standard, the Committee rejects that submission.
The Committee has reviewed and considered the relevant case law and the prior decisions of this Committee referenced in Mr. Pappas’s materials. The Dudas decision is distinguishable as there were “a number of apparent contraventions”, which the Committee considered “too numerous” to forego referring the matter to prosecution. With respect to the Taylor matter, it is true that one member of the Committee commented that “clerical errors are still errors, and minor errors can’t simply be overlooked”. Respectfully, despite this absolute statement, the case law is clear that at this stage of the Committee’s proceedings, the Committee retains discretion not to refer a matter to prosecution if it considers the apparent violationsde minimis.
Concerning the submissions made by Mr. Phillips about a “clerical error,” inPhillips v Ottawa (Elections Compliance Audit Committee), the Superior Court stated that “[a]n error that is not a mere “typographical error” but is a substantive inaccuracy in calculation or reporting is sufficient to clear the very low hurdle at the first step of the s. 88.33 procedure” (emphasis added). This suggests that there are certain types of typographical, clerical or trivial errors that are so minor that they do not even contravene the MEA to begin with. One example would be the errors that Candidate Harris made inLancaster v Compliance Audit Committee, 2012 ONSC 5629, where a candidate accidentally listed 2 associated corporate donors under Table 2 of Form 4, but had accurate information otherwise. The Court found no violation of the MEA. As such, at thisfinalstage of the Committee’s procedure, and in line with the case law, there is discretion not to refer a matter to prosecution in the face of an apparent violation the Committee considers insufficient to merit that step.
In the particular circumstances before us, the Committee considers the apparent violation to bede minimisand that commencing legal proceedings is not warranted.
First, Mr. Menard has accepted the Audit Report, demonstrating accountability. The identified issue pertains to the reuse of campaign materials, which resulted in a discrepancy in reported expenses. The Audit confirmed that Mr. Menard’s campaign did not suffer from systemic or intentional violations.
Second, the Committee considers the apparent violationde minimisbased on the following circumstances, taken together: 1) the dollar amount, $310.98, is fairly low; 2) the underreporting did not result in Mr. Menard exceeding his expense limits; 3) Mr. Menard did not exceed the maximum contribution limit for a candidate and/or spouse; and 4) the Committee does not find that Mr. Menard gained an unfair advantage due to the apparent violation.
Third, from a transparency and accountability perspective, Mr. Menard’s campaign finances have been heavily scrutinized, both in this process and the media. Although this factor on its own would not cause the Committee to abstain from commencing legal proceedings, when considered together with the previous points, the Committee is of the view that the MEA’s transparency and accountability objective have been served.
Had Mr. Menard’s violations been of a sort that could, in the eyes of a reasonable member of the public, resulted in an unfair advantage, or one that might impact the integrity of the election process, our decision might have been different. This is not the case.
In the result, the Committee is driven to the conclusion that, weighing these factors, the public interest is best served by not commencing legal proceedings in these circumstances.
